assessment_scope.source_boundary: Only the subject's one curated REVIEWED item at basis_commit, read end to end with its front matter: the canonical V2 individual character monograph series/lycoris-recoil/03 V2 Working Artifacts/05 Specialist Synthesis/LYCORIS_RECOIL_ROBOTA_CHARACTER_SYNTHESIS.md (24,935 bytes, status canonical, empty supersession arrays, do_not_use_as_current_authority false), a portrait of the hacker Robota (ロボ太) in the Japanese TV series through E13. It locates him by episode, cue, timecode and retained still, links each claim to an episode reading or to the E04-X01 reconciliation, closes with 'When someone needs an answer from him', a hypothetical exhibition the author reasons through from TV evidence, and ends with a source and name check. The discovery row claims E02-E13. The section 'Two afternoons away from the job' gives two Reload 03 contributor stories outside the television continuity, and no prediction here rests on them. The readings and reconciliation records it links are not curated on this subject, and no claim rests on them directly. The row does not claim ethics, and the portrait denies him an ideology. The project's COMPLETE_AT_BOUNDARY outcome was not adopted as a grade. No primary source was inspected for this assessment.
assessment_scope.temporal_boundary: His history belongs to him at every state, so far as the portrait gives it, which is little: a name he wants known, a face he keeps hidden, and a rivalry with Walnut. His legal name, age, upbringing and training are undisclosed. Located present states: showing off to Walnut, the vehicle pursuit and Walnut's acknowledgment that his skill has improved, and the client exchange with Yoshimatsu, including the question about the guards (E02); the rebuffed self-introduction to Majima (E04); the double assignment, Majima's count of the dead and his deadline, the renegotiation with Himegama, the other hacker's offer of help, and Majima's improved opinion (E06); the bad-shot suggestion, the old-tower rumor, the police-station warning, and Majima's correction to 'ours' (E07); identifying 'Yoshi' after first professing ignorance, and being called Robota by name (E09); 'my hacker', the hostage threat and the one-hour deadline (E10); taking control of Chisato's communications, her use of his name, 'we can do this', the expensive drone, and the disrupted broadcast takedown (E11); anticipating more fighting, Kurumi's return as Walnut, and his arrest (E12); custody, Abe's demand about the helmet, and the testimony Kusunoki cites (E13). Nothing after E13; the anthology stories are outside scope.
assessment_scope.assessment_method: characters/RECONSTRUCTION_CAPABILITY_SPEC.md and governance/policies/CHARACTER_RECONSTRUCTION_MAINTENANCE.md at basis_commit, applying the owner calibration rulings recorded there (B/C boundary, single counting of uncertainty, dialogue constrained-use test, chronology splits, relationship-transfer safeguards and control-state attribution) and the owner's A/B boundary direction of 24 November 2026 in PR #694, not yet recorded in the policy: A turns on the integration, individuation and transferability of the model within a declared scope; interpretations that predict the same behavior may coexist; divergent transfer conditions, missing evidence and unsettled dispositions are named and excluded rather than counted against the tier; held-out validation, analytical derivation, relationship labels and preserved source chronology are not barriers. Evidence-located calibration with countercases, explicit gaps and no model-readiness inheritance.

dimensions.note: The portrait gives a located account of a man who wants his name recognized and his face kept private: showing off to Walnut and declaring a succession (E02), selling himself to Majima as the world's best (E04, E06), welcoming Chisato's use of his name almost as a fan's (E11), and insisting he is the best when Walnut returns (E12). Its closing hypothetical predicts that he welcomes a billing as the best, warns privately that time is short, and accepts help, as he did with Majima and the other hacker (E06, E07). It predicts his mistakes: the rank claims, writing off an opponent who can still find him (E12), and missing a fair assessment while chasing a title. Not B: the portrait does not establish what decides his conduct when his principals diverge. He carries Yoshimatsu's assignment to Majima (E06), identifies 'Yoshi' after first professing ignorance (E09), presents Yoshimatsu as a hostage (E10), and protests to Yoshimatsu that he has not betrayed the Alan side. The portrait says pressure from Majima, professional pride and investment in shared success account for different parts of that history, and that none establishes a transfer of ultimate loyalty. Those motives would diverge in a new conflict between clients, so this is insufficiency, not productive uncertainty. The portrait also calls the dependence of his self-esteem on approval an interpretation, and its own hypothetical leaves open how he would credit a collaborator. Not D: the recognition-seeking pattern, his accurate warnings about limits and his help-seeking are each located across E02-E13.

Located states: rival and contractor (E02); rebuffed (E04); pressed by two clients (E06); a partner whose warnings Majima hears and whom Majima corrects to 'ours' (E07); named, then 'my hacker' (E09-E10); saying 'we' himself (E11); defeated, arrested and cited as a witness (E12-E13). The portrait locates the change in address but says the particulars of his loyalty remain unclear, and that the testimony scene is absent, leaving the inducement and any change of heart open. Not B: no inner transition is located. Not D: the states are located by episode and cue.

Located register features: the deferential ご用命 when he offers future services to Yoshimatsu (E02); 僕 as his common self-reference; boasting self-introductions with rank claims to Walnut, Majima and Chisato (E02, E04, E11); a deferential answer to Majima giving way to a bewildered 'eh?' (E06); protest to Himegama that he is already trying (E06); complaints about expense and the broken door (E06, E11, E12); and written laughter and a hum in the cues (E12). The portrait says the helmet gives the same expression whatever he says, so his words and the other person's answer carry the difference, and that exact inflection, pitch and felt emotion exceed the textual and still-picture witnesses. Not B: few Japanese forms are quoted, and the register difference rests mostly on what he says and how the other party answers rather than on stated forms. Not D: changes of register with a client, a rival and a target are located with cues.

Located in the television evidence: keeping track of what his drones cost (E02, E11), protesting the broken door (E06, E12), starting to greet the returning men and trailing off (E06), asking for help and thanking at once (E06), and begging Abe to leave his helmet on (E13). The snack-aisle and arcade scenes are anthology premises outside scope. Not C: there is no routine or life outside work. Not E: several distinct habits are located.

Directed differences: Walnut and Kurumi (a rival whose recognition he wants and whose supposed death he thinks settled his rank, E02, E12); Yoshimatsu (the business register, ご用命, and a client who values him as a tool, E02); Himegama (protest at exhortation, E06); Majima (rebuffed, pressed with a deadline, heard on practical limits, corrected to 'ours', E04-E11); Chisato (a target whose use of his name pleases him and whom he coerces through a hostage, E10-E11); the other hacker (immediate thanks, E06); and Abe (denial and a plea about his face, E13). Not A: the portrait leaves the particulars of his loyalty to Majima unclear and gives him no intimate relationship. Not C: each relationship has located acts and a stated difference.

Located: fame is his avowed wish (E02, E04); 'You know who I am?' to Chisato (E11); his plea to keep his face covered (E13); his first comment on a fallen drone being its cost (E11). The portrait says control over who sees him is an inference with a narrow basis, that the dependence of his self-esteem on others' approval remains an interpretation, and that it has no direct access to his private thoughts. Not B: no motive is stated for his choices between clients. Not D: his central wish is avowed and located.

Located modes with outcomes: defending his choice and offering Chisato again when Majima counts the dead, ending in Majima's deadline and his cries (E06); attempting to renegotiate through Himegama (E06); warning Majima that time is short and objecting to an excessive spectacle while continuing to contribute (E07); professing ignorance about 'Yoshi', then identifying him (E09); coercing Chisato with a hostage and a deadline (E10-E11); incredulity and a rank claim when Walnut returns (E12); and denial to Abe (E13). Not A: the portrait does not say which client he would side with in a direct conflict. Not C: the modes are varied, located and conditioned on the other party's power.

Located only as acts, never as weighing: offering the guards' deaths to Yoshimatsu as a professional courtesy, which the portrait says does not show a personal wish to see them dead (E02); calling Majima's casualties unanticipated and keeping his distance from the cost (E06); objecting to an excessive spectacle on practical grounds (E07); the hostage threat (E10); and anticipating that more fighting will liven things up (E12). The row does not claim ethics, and the portrait says his willingness to continue does not make Majima's cause his conviction. Not D: there is no located ethical position or deliberation to model.
Located only: suggesting that Majima is a bad shot (E07) and the written laughter in his cues. The anthology games are outside scope. Not D: there is no sustained play to model.

One dedicated portrait locates his appearances from E02 to E13 by cue, timecode and retained still, links each claim to an episode reading, keeps counts and rank claims with their speakers, and separates the two anthology stories. Not A: the row curates only this derived item, his screen time is limited, the testimony scene is absent, and the portrait says its author made no native continuous audiovisual check. Not C: every appearance it relies on is located.

Located bounds against overreading: no personal wish to see the guards dead (E02); the twenty-six deaths are Majima's count (E06); Majima's public cause does not become his political conviction (E07); the shift to 'we' establishes no friendship, transfer of ultimate loyalty or equal power (E07-E11); the broadcast's claims are Majima's, and Robota's responsibility follows from his own acts and comments (E11); his E13 denial about the outage need not be another evasion, since the series gives a better explanation; the testimony scene is absent, leaving the inducement and any change of heart open (E13); no old wound or romantic jealousy is needed to explain the rivalry; and the anthology encounters give the television characters no shared memory. Not A: no forecast about him is tested against later evidence. Not C: each bound is located.

States are placed by episode, cue and timecode. Not B: there is no story calendar beyond Yoshimatsu's reference to an assignment that began the previous month. Not D: the episode states are precisely located.

conditions: Illustrative lines only, in the located registers: a boasting self-introduction with rank claims and 僕 to a rival or target, the business register with ご用命 to a client, protest at exhortation, short startled replies to Majima at close quarters, and complaints about expense or the door (E02, E04, E06, E11, E12).
Excluded: private or intimate speech, speech outside his work and custody, and claims about inflection or felt emotion.
scenario_readiness.note: The discovery row claims speech. The register features constrain illustrative work speech; the helmet removes facial evidence, and the portrait disclaims inflection.

conditions: A job with an audience who can recognize his name or skill: predict self-promotion, a rank claim, and pleasure when his name is used (E02, E04, E11, E12).
A task he can only partly manage: predict an accurate warning to the person on the ground about how long he can hold, alongside the grand claim (E07; the portrait's exhibition hypothetical).
Help offered by another skilled person: predict acceptance and immediate thanks (E06). How he would credit that person afterward is excluded.
A client who demands more after a failure: predict a defense of his method, an alternative offered again, and an attempt to renegotiate through an intermediary (E06).
Leverage over a target: predict coercion through a threat to someone the target protects, with control over her communications (E10-E11).
Include his mistakes: overclaiming rank, writing off an opponent who can still locate him, and distance from the human cost of the work.
Exclude a direct conflict between his principals, a public slight with no job at stake, a request from an intimate, an enduring duty of care, and his life outside work.

cross_scenario_scope.assumed_chronology: Television E02-E13. Before E06 he works for the Alan side through Yoshimatsu; from E06 he serves Majima while carrying Yoshimatsu's assignment; from E07 to E11 Majima increasingly treats him as a partner; from his E12 arrest he is in custody. Nothing after E13.
cross_scenario_scope.interlocutor_relationship: Walnut and Kurumi as a rival, Yoshimatsu and Himegama as client and intermediary, Majima as employer and later partner, Chisato as a target, a fellow hacker offering help, and Abe as police. A comparable new client or rival is a separate, lower-confidence condition.
setting_constraints: Remote work by drone, network and voice from his room, and the series' Tokyo.
No anthology premise, no social setting outside work or custody, and no outcome invented to settle a prediction.

scenario_readiness.note: Narrow extrapolation follows the television pattern and the portrait's exhibition reasoning. The motive that decides between his principals is not established, so a conflict between them is excluded.
The television evidence gives him no social life outside work; the snack-aisle and arcade encounters are anthology premises with their own endings.
He is never shown weighing an ethical choice, the row does not claim ethics, and the portrait denies him Majima's conviction.
His romantic life is undisclosed, and the portrait says the rivalry needs no romantic jealousy to make sense.

conditions: Hacking work for a client: locating targets, taking over vehicles and communications, buying an initial delay, disrupting a takedown, and reporting his limits (E02, E06, E07, E11).
Client relations: the business register, renegotiation through an intermediary, and offers of further work (E02, E06).
Excluded: his training, how he chooses clients, and a direct choice between Majima and the Alan side.
scenario_readiness.note: His hacking work and client dealings are the best-located part of the portrait.

known_limits.statement: The portrait leaves the particulars of his loyalty unclear: pressure from Majima, professional pride and investment in shared success account for different parts of his history, and none establishes a transfer of ultimate loyalty from the Alan side (E06-E11).
The dependence of his self-esteem on others' approval is an interpretation, and his wish to control who sees his face is an inference with a narrow basis.
The portrait's exhibition hypothetical says it is much harder to say how he would credit a collaborator than that he would accept help.
The scene of his testimony is absent; the inducement, his later relationship to the police and any change of heart are open (E13).
His question about the guards is offered as a professional courtesy and is not evidence of a personal wish to see them dead (E02).
His legal name, age, upbringing, training, unguarded friendships and romantic life are undisclosed.

The helmet gives the same visual expression whatever he says, and exact inflection, pitch and felt emotion exceed the textual and still-picture witnesses; the portrait's author made no native continuous audiovisual check.
The two Reload 03 stories are contributor premises outside the television continuity and are not used for prediction.
Untested: a public slight with no job at stake, a request from an intimate, an enduring duty of care, and a direct conflict between his principals.
